<color=#3366CC>natural gas</color>, and <color=#3366CC>coal</color> in the past decades. The fire in a <color=#3366CC>power station</color> is used to heat water, creating steam that drives
<color=#3366CC>turbines</color>. The turbines then spin an <color=#3366CC>electric generator</color> to produce electricity. Fire is also used to provide <color=#3366CC>mechanical</color>
<color=#3366CC>work</color> directly by <color=#3366CC>thermal expansion</color>, in both external and <color=#3366CC>internal combustion engines</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>unburnable</color> solid remains of a combustible material left after a fire is called clinker if its <color=#3366CC>melting point</color> is below the
flame temperature, so that it fuses and then solidifies as it cools, and ash if its melting point is above the flame
temperature.
Physical properties
Chemistry

Fire is a chemical process in which a <color=#3366CC>fuel</color> and an <color=#3366CC>oxidizing agent</color> react, yielding <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color> and <color=#3366CC>water</color>. This
process, known as a <color=#3366CC>combustion reaction</color>, does not proceed directly and involves <color=#3366CC>intermediates</color>. Although the oxidizing
agent is typically <color=#3366CC>oxygen</color>, other compounds can fulfill the role. For instance, chlorine trifluoride is able to ignite <color=#3366CC>sand</color>.
Fires start when a flammable or a combustible material, in combination with a sufficient quantity of an <color=#3366CC>oxidizer</color> such as
oxygen gas or another oxygen-rich compound (though non-oxygen oxidizers exist, such as chlorine), is exposed to a
source of heat or ambient <color=#3366CC>temperature</color> above the flash point for the <color=#3366CC>fuel</color>/oxidizer mix, and can sustain a rate of rapid
oxidation that produces a <color=#3366CC>chain reaction</color>. This is commonly called the fire tetrahedron. Fire cannot exist without all of
these elements in place and in the right proportions. For example, a flammable liquid will start burning only if the fuel
and oxygen are in the right proportions. Some fuel-oxygen mixes may require a <color=#3366CC>catalyst</color>, a substance that is not
consumed, when added, in any <color=#3366CC>chemical</color> reaction during combustion, but which enables the reactants to combust more
readily.
Once ignited, a chain reaction occurs whereby fires can sustain their own heat through the continued release of heat
energy during combustion and may propagate, provided there is a continuous supply of an oxidizer and fuel. If the
oxidizer is oxygen from the surrounding air, the presence of a force of <color=#3366CC>gravity</color>, or of some similar force caused by
acceleration, is necessary to produce <color=#3366CC>convection</color>, which removes combustion products and brings a supply of oxygen
to the fire. Without gravity, a fire rapidly surrounds itself with its own combustion products and non-oxidizing gases from
the air, which exclude oxygen and the fire. Because of this, the risk of fire in a <color=#3366CC>spacecraft</color> is small when it is coasting in
inertial flight. This does not apply if oxygen is supplied to the fire by some process other than thermal convection.
Fire can be extinguished by removing any one of the elements of the fire tetrahedron. Consider a natural gas flame,
such as from a stove-top burner. Any of the following can extinguish the fire:
• turning off the gas supply, which removes the fuel source;
• covering the flame completely, which smothers the flame as the combustion both uses the available oxidizer (the
oxygen in the air) and displaces it from the area around the flame with CO2;
• application of an inert gas such as <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color>, smothering the flame by displacing the available oxidizer;
• application of water, which removes heat from the fire faster than the fire can produce it (similarly, blowing hard on
a flame will displace the heat of the currently burning gas from its fuel source, to the same end); or
• application of a retardant chemical such as Halon (largely banned in some countries ) to the flame, which retards
the chemical reaction itself until the rate of combustion is too slow to maintain the chain reaction.
In contrast, fire is intensified by increasing the overall combustion rate. Methods to do this include balancing the input of
fuel and oxidizer to <color=#3366CC>stoichiometric</color> proportions, increasing fuel and oxidizer input in this balanced mix, increasing the
ambient temperature so the fire's own heat is better able to sustain combustion, or providing a catalyst, a non-reactant
medium in which the fuel and oxidizer can more readily react.
Flame
A diffusion flame is a mixture of reacting gases and solids emitting visible, <color=#3366CC>infrared</color>, and sometimes <color=#3366CC>ultraviolet</color> light, the
<color=#3366CC>frequency spectrum</color> of which depends on the <color=#3366CC>chemical composition</color> of the burning material and intermediate reaction
products. During the burning of <color=#3366CC>hydrocarbons</color>, for example wood, or the incomplete <color=#3366CC>combustion</color> of gas, <color=#3366CC>incandescent</color>
solid particles called <color=#3366CC>soot</color> produce the familiar red-orange glow of "fire". This light has a continuous spectrum. Complete
combustion of gas has a dim blue color due to the emission of single-wavelength radiation from various electron
transitions in the excited molecules formed in the flame.
Usually oxygen is involved, but <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color> burning in <color=#3366CC>chlorine</color> also produces a flame, producing <color=#3366CC>hydrogen chloride</color> (HCl).
Other possible combinations producing flames, amongst many, are <color=#3366CC>fluorine</color> with hydrogen, and <color=#3366CC>hydrazine</color> with
dinitrogen tetroxide. Hydrogen and hydrazine/UDMH flames are similarly pale blue, while burning <color=#3366CC>boron</color> and its
compounds, evaluated in mid-20th century as a high energy fuel for <color=#3366CC>jet</color> and <color=#3366CC>rocket engines</color>, emits intense green flame,
leading to its informal nickname of "Green Dragon".
The glow of a flame is complex. <color=#3366CC>Black-body radiation</color> is emitted from soot, gas, and fuel particles, though the soot
particles are too small to behave like perfect blackbodies. There is also <color=#3366CC>photon</color> emission by de-excited <color=#3366CC>atoms</color> and
<color=#3366CC>molecules</color> in the gases. Much of the radiation is emitted in the visible and infrared bands. The color depends on
temperature for the black-body radiation, and on chemical makeup for the <color=#3366CC>emission spectra</color>.
The common distribution of a flame under normal gravity conditions depends on <color=#3366CC>convection</color>, as soot tends to rise to the
top of a general flame, as in a <color=#3366CC>candle</color> in normal gravity conditions, making it yellow. In microgravity or zero gravity, such
as an environment in <color=#3366CC>outer space</color>, convection no longer occurs, and the flame becomes spherical, with a tendency to
become more blue and more efficient (although it may go out if not moved steadily, as the CO2 from combustion does
not disperse as readily in microgravity, and tends to smother the flame). There are several possible explanations for
this difference, the most likely being that the temperature is sufficiently uniform that soot does not form and complete
combustion occurs.
Experiments by <color=#3366CC>NASA</color> reveal that diffusion flames in microgravity allow more soot to be completely oxidized after they
are produced than diffusion flames on Earth, because of a series of mechanisms that behave differently in micro gravity
when compared to normal gravity conditions. These discoveries have potential applications in <color=#3366CC>applied science</color> and
industry, especially concerning fuel efficiency.
Typical adiabatic temperatures
The adiabatic flame temperature of a given fuel-oxidizer pair is the temperature at which the gases achieve stable
combustion.

Fire science
Fire science is a branch of physical science which includes fire behavior, dynamics, and <color=#3366CC>combustion</color>. Applications of
fire science include fire protection, fire investigation, and <color=#3366CC>wildfire</color> management.
Ecology
Every natural ecosystem on land has its own fire regime, and the organisms in those ecosystems are adapted to or
dependent upon that fire regime. Fire creates a mosaic of different <color=#3366CC>habitat</color> patches, each at a different stage of
<color=#3366CC>succession</color>. Different species of plants, animals, and microbes specialize in exploiting a particular stage, and by
creating these different types of patches, fire allows a greater number of species to exist within a landscape. <color=#3366CC>Changes</color>
<color=#3366CC>in climate</color> can significantly modify the risk for wildfires in a region.
Firefighting
<color=#3366CC>Fire fighting</color> services are provided in most developed areas to extinguish or contain uncontrolled fires. Trained
<color=#3366CC>firefighters</color> use fire apparatus, water supply resources such as water mains and <color=#3366CC>fire hydrants</color>, or they might use A and
B class foam depending on what is feeding the fire.
The early detection of a wildfire outbreak can be performed by a fire lookout observing from a tower constructed for that
purpose. The use of these towers peaked in 1938 and has been in decline since then; most fire surveillance work is
now performed using infrared sensors and aircraft. Fire suppression aircraft guided by a lookout can be used to help
manage wildfires. These are primarily used in support of ground crews
Management, prevention and protection systems
Controlling a fire to optimize its size, shape, and intensity is generally called fire management, and the more advanced
forms of it, as traditionally (and sometimes still) practiced by skilled cooks, <color=#3366CC>blacksmiths</color>, ironmasters, and others, are
highly <color=#3366CC>skilled</color> activities. They include knowledge of which fuel to burn; how to arrange the fuel; how to stoke the fire both
in early phases and in maintenance phases; how to modulate the heat, flame, and smoke as suited to the desired
application; how best to bank a fire to be revived later; how to choose, design, or modify stoves, fireplaces, bakery
ovens, or industrial furnaces; and so on. Detailed expositions of fire management are available in various books on
blacksmithing, skilled <color=#3366CC>camping</color> or <color=#3366CC>military scouting</color>, and <color=#3366CC>domestic arts</color>.
Wildfire prevention programs around the world may employ techniques such as wildland fire use and prescribed or
<color=#3366CC>controlled burns</color>. Wildland fire use refers to any fire of natural causes that is monitored but allowed to burn. Controlled
burns are fires ignited by government agencies under less dangerous weather conditions.
Fire prevention is intended to reduce sources of ignition. Fire prevention also includes education on how to avoid
causing fires. Buildings, especially schools and tall buildings, often conduct fire drills to inform and prepare citizens on
how to react to a building fire. Purposely starting destructive fires constitutes <color=#3366CC>arson</color> and is a crime in most jurisdictions.
Model <color=#3366CC>building codes</color> require passive fire protection and active fire protection systems to minimize damage resulting
from a fire. A common form of active fire protection is fire sprinklers. To maximize passive fire protection of buildings,
building materials and furnishings in most developed countries are tested for fire-resistance, combustibility and
flammability. <color=#3366CC>Upholstery</color>, carpeting and <color=#3366CC>plastics</color> used in vehicles and vessels are also tested.
Studies have found that functioning <color=#3366CC>smoke detectors</color> reduce the risk of <color=#3366CC>death</color> in a fire by 50%, and sprinkler systems
can reduce mortality by 100%. Fire-resistant clothing, beds, and sofas have also been shown to reduce injuries
resulting from fires. In the United States, the leading cause of residential fires is <color=#3366CC>cooking</color> equipment, particularly
cooking left unattended. It is estimated that <color=#3366CC>cigarettes</color> and other smoking materials are responsible for about 28% of
home fires involving the ignition of upholstered furniture, and for approximately 58% of the fatalities in such fires. Fires
started by cigarettes are also more lethal and have higher mortality rates than fires that spread from open flames. The
adoption of fire-safe cigarettes has been associated with a 45% reduction in fires caused by cigarettes.
Where fire prevention and fire protection have failed to prevent damage, <color=#3366CC>fire insurance</color> can mitigate the financial
impact.
In culture
Fire has been an importance element of human culture since the <color=#3366CC>Lower Paleolithic</color>. Archaeological evidence
demonstrates that fire worship has been widely practiced since <color=#3366CC>prehistory</color>, with dedicated structures found dating from
at least the <color=#3366CC>Chalcolithic</color> period. The religion of <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrianism</color> is closely linked to this practice. In some societies fire
was a deity, while others viewed it as the <color=#3366CC>manifestation of the divine</color>. The fire in a hearth was perceived as symbolic of
the Heavenly Fire, and thus is considered a sacred component by fire-worshipping cultures. The origin of fire became a
subject of mythology. In ancient Greek culture, the Titan god <color=#3366CC>Prometheus</color> was responsible for stealing heavenly fire
and giving it to humanity.
The use of a pyre as a <color=#3366CC>funerary</color> practice dates back to at least the Ancient Roman period in the West, and to about
4,000 years ago on the Indian subcontinent. <color=#3366CC>Cremation</color> of corpses is a tradition long practiced in some cultures,
including Hindu. After early religious resistance in some countries, in the 19th century this practice became more
widespread and is now commonplace. In some nations, suicide by self-immolation remains common.
The symbology of fire remains important to the present day. Where wood is plentiful, the <color=#3366CC>bonfire</color> can be used for
celebration purposes, in many cases as part of a tradition. An example is Guy Fawkes Night in England. The <color=#3366CC>barbecue</color>
is a fire-based cultural tradition in the United States. The fiery ignition of <color=#3366CC>fireworks</color> has become a modern tradition to
celebrate the <color=#3366CC>New Year</color>'s arrival. In contrast, <color=#3366CC>book burning</color> has been used as a form of protest, whether for political,
religious, or moral reasons. The act of "burning in effigy" has a similar role, as in the annual burning of Judas ritual.
Humans lack an instinctual fascination with fire, yet in modern societies, adults can become drawn to it out of curiosity.
In societies that rely on daily fire use, children lose interest in fire around age 7 due to regular exposure. <color=#3366CC>Arson</color> is the
act of intentionally setting fire to a property. A separate but related behavior is <color=#3366CC>pyromania</color>, which is classified as an
impulse-control disorder where individuals repeatedly fail to resist impulses to start fires deliberately. In contrast is
pyrophobia, an irrational fear of fire. This <color=#3366CC>anxiety disorder</color> is a less common phobia.
